title: Projection
description: Choose output attribute roles while respecting set duplicate elimination, distinguish SQL bag projection from relational projection, and preserve the intended result grain.
notes:
## Projection chooses the attribute roles

Projection in relational algebra returns a relation containing specified attributes from an input relation. Its conventional symbol is pi. If Student has id, name, department, and gpa, projecting onto department returns the department values represented in the input. It does not apply a grade threshold or create a new department merely because a label is selected.

The result's structure is determined by the chosen attribute list. Selecting two attributes produces degree two in that result, even if the source has four or more attributes. The input relation remains unchanged. Projection is a logical operation deriving another result rather than an instruction to delete source columns or alter persistent table definitions.

## Pure projection follows set semantics

A mathematical relation is a set of tuples, so equal projected tuples appear once. Suppose three identified students have departments Computing, Computing, and History. Their department projection contains Computing and History. The two Computing student facts remain distinct in the source because their full tuples or keys differ, but the selected one-attribute output values are equal.

This reduction is not a row predicate. No student was deemed ineligible through a condition. The selected tuple values simply coincide after identifying attributes have been removed. It is therefore inaccurate to say pure projection always preserves cardinality or behaves exactly like selection. It changes structure, and set duplicate elimination can change how many result tuples remain.

## SQL needs an explicit duplicate policy

An ordinary SQL SELECT department can return Computing twice under its usual bag-like result behaviour. SELECT DISTINCT department requests one row for each distinct selected value combination. This more closely models the classical projection in the stated nonmissing fixture. SQL's practical type and NULL rules still need their own interpretation rather than being assumed identical to every classical abstraction.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT department
FROM students
ORDER BY department;
```

The query asks which department values occur among the source student facts. It is not a complete department catalogue and does not include a valid catalogue department with no students. If the task asks for all defined departments, start from the authoritative catalogue population instead. Projection reports represented values from its actual input.

## DISTINCT compares the complete selected tuple

Selecting DISTINCT department and campus gives one row per distinct pair, not one row per department alone. Computing at North and Computing at South remain separate output tuples because the campus values differ. A student identifier included in the projection can preserve each unique student row even when all displayed department and campus labels match.

Adding an identifier merely to make every row distinct therefore changes the requested output. If the requirement is distinct department-campus combinations, selecting id as well does not implement it. Decide the result grain first, then choose the attributes and duplicate policy. A plausible-looking list can still answer the wrong question if its identity differs from the task.

## Retained keys preserve source tuple distinctions

Under a guaranteed nonmissing unique source key, a projection retaining that key cannot collapse two different source tuples into one equal projected tuple. Each key value distinguishes its source fact. A projection that omits the key may or may not reduce cardinality depending on the remaining values and constraints. The key guarantee explains why, rather than an assumption based on current names.

A current sample with unique names does not establish name as a schema key for every allowed state. Another student may legitimately share a name later. When a report must list individual students, retain their intended identities. When it intentionally reports unique descriptive combinations, omit irrelevant identity columns and accept the set-grain change deliberately.

## Projection and selection compose carefully

A high-GPA department report can first restrict students by the grade predicate and then project distinct departments. If the projection removes gpa before a later selection needs it, that later predicate is no longer directly expressible over the narrowed result. Operation order and available attributes must preserve every role required by the remaining conditions.

Some algebraic reorderings are valid when the projected attributes retain all predicate inputs and the relevant assumptions hold. They are logical equivalences, not a guarantee that SQL physically executes clauses in a particular textual order. Explain the intended final population and structure before drawing conclusions about optimizer choices or assuming a rewritten query is faster.

## Attribute names and order form an output contract

An explicit SQL projection states selected roles and their presentation order. A consumer expecting student_id followed by department should not silently receive every source column through SELECT star. A later source-schema addition can widen a star-based result and affect positional consumers or expose data they did not need. Explicit selected columns keep the requested shape visible.

Aliases can make output names understandable without changing source names or values. Calling an expression total_score should reflect its actual meaning and units. Projection in the basic algebra selects attributes; SQL can also compute expressions in its selected list, which is a richer facility. Keep the simple conceptual operation distinct from every feature the SQL SELECT clause can express.

## Missing values require SQL-specific care

SQL DISTINCT has specified handling for repeated NULLs, unlike ordinary equality predicates where NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN. A nullable department projection can therefore include one NULL output value when absence is represented in the source. It is incorrect to claim duplicate elimination becomes undefined because ordinary NULL equality is not TRUE.

The report must decide whether missing departments belong in the requested population. WHERE department IS NOT NULL can exclude those source rows before projection. Replacing NULL with the ordinary string Unassigned can change which values collide if that same string is also a real label. State the domain and display policy rather than silently treating absence, empty strings, and placeholders as interchangeable.

## Empty inputs retain result structure

Projecting an empty student relation onto department yields no department tuples, but the selected attribute role remains defined. An empty result does not imply a degree-zero relation. Conversely, selecting no attributes is a special formal construction not equivalent to an ordinary one-column SQL result with NULL. The practical exercises use explicit nonempty projection lists and documented output columns.

A scalar COUNT query over an empty projection can return one row containing zero, while the projection itself returns no rows. Keep those output cardinalities separate. A report's expected data should state whether it lists combinations or summarizes their count instead of treating every zero-row or zero-valued output as the same result.

## Projection does not authorize access

Selecting fewer columns can reduce unnecessary data in a response, but a client-side projection alone is not proof that protected attributes are inaccessible through another request. Trusted access enforcement belongs at the actual data boundary. An application promising restricted student data needs appropriate authorization independent of whether one example query happens to request only a harmless-looking label.

Similarly, removing a column from a query does not delete the stored information or implement a retention policy. The operation derives a result. Persistent schema changes, data removal, and access control each have different requirements and verification boundaries. Avoid turning a clear projection lesson into unsupported claims about production security or physical storage cleanup.

## Validate grain and duplicate behaviour explicitly

Use several students in one department, the same department across different campuses, distinct student identities sharing all selected descriptions, and an empty input. For a filtered projection, include an excluded campus or status that otherwise contributes a unique combination. These fixtures expose missing DISTINCT, an accidentally retained id, or a population predicate applied to the wrong input.

The exercises verify distinct department values and distinct active department-campus pairs on isolated SQL data. They retain a clear nonmissing domain so the selected set semantics are directly visible. Exact MySQL/provider execution and production authority remain separate evidence. Projection becomes useful when the chosen attributes, input population, duplicate policy, identity changes, and output shape all match the question instead of merely returning fewer columns.

questions.question_text: What does the Projection operation (π) do?
options: Filters rows by a condition
Selects a subset of columns from a relation
Joins two relations together
Sorts a relation's rows
questions.explanation: Projection narrows by COLUMNS, keeping only the specified attributes.

questions.question_text: Why does `SELECT DISTINCT department FROM students` more accurately model relational-algebra Projection than plain `SELECT department FROM students`?
options: DISTINCT has no real effect on the result
Pure relational algebra projection removes duplicate rows automatically (a relation is a set), while plain SQL SELECT does not by default
DISTINCT makes the query run in a different order
SQL never allows duplicate rows in any query result
questions.explanation: SQL relations behave like multisets by default; DISTINCT is needed to match the pure set-based behavior of algebraic projection.

questions.question_text: For a projection of a strict relation retaining its guaranteed unique nonmissing key, can duplicate elimination merge different source tuples?
options: Always fewer, due to duplicate elimination
The same number of rows, since a unique key guarantees no duplicates can arise
Always exactly one row
This cannot be determined
questions.explanation: The retained key distinguishes every source tuple, so the projected cardinality stays the same under those assumptions.

questions.question_text: What is a common way Selection and Projection are used together?
options: They can never be combined in one query
Selection filters to the rows of interest, then Projection narrows to just the columns needed to answer the question
Projection must always run before any Selection, with no exceptions
They perform the exact same function and are interchangeable
questions.explanation: Combining filter-then-narrow-columns is one of the most common patterns for answering real queries.

questions.question_text: In relational algebra, is a relation formally treated as a set or a bag (multiset) of tuples?
options: A bag, allowing duplicates
A set, meaning no duplicate tuples are allowed
Neither — relations have no formal structure
This varies arbitrarily by textbook with no real consensus
questions.explanation: The classical relational model defines a relation as a SET of tuples, which is exactly why projection in the algebra removes duplicates automatically.

questions.question_text: Does Projection ever filter which ROWS appear, the way Selection does?
options: Yes, Projection and Selection filter rows identically
Not directly — any row-count reduction from Projection comes only as a side effect of duplicate elimination after removing columns, not from a row condition
Projection removes exactly half the rows every time
Projection always returns all rows unchanged, with duplicates included
questions.explanation: Projection's job is picking columns; any fewer rows in the output are purely an artifact of resulting duplicate rows collapsing together.

questions.question_text: Which SQL feature is the direct equivalent of relational algebra's Projection?
options: The WHERE clause
The selected attribute list supplies projection, with DISTINCT needed when SQL output must match classical set duplicate elimination
The ORDER BY clause
The FROM clause
questions.explanation: The SQL column list alone ordinarily retains duplicate output rows; exact classical projection also needs the appropriate set semantics.

questions.question_text: Why might forgetting DISTINCT in a query intended to model pure Projection produce a misleading result?
options: It never produces a misleading result
The query could return the same value many times over instead of the distinct set of values a textbook projection would produce
DISTINCT is required by SQL syntax and its absence causes a syntax error
Forgetting DISTINCT always returns zero rows
questions.explanation: Without DISTINCT, repeated values remain in the output, which doesn't match the duplicate-free guarantee of true relational-algebra projection.

questions.question_text: Three identified students have departments X,X,Y. What is the classical department projection?
options: X,X,Y always
X and Y once each
Only X
Three new department entities
questions.explanation: Pure projection returns a set of selected tuples.

questions.question_text: Does SELECT DISTINCT department, campus deduplicate only department?
options: Yes; only the first expression matters
Only if campus is text
No; it compares complete selected pairs
Only if ids are omitted
questions.explanation: The selected tuple defines equality for DISTINCT.

questions.question_text: What can happen when id is added to a distinct department report?
options: It always removes more rows
It changes source departments
Separate student identities prevent the intended department-only collapse
It makes every key nullable
questions.explanation: Adding identity changes result grain.

questions.question_text: Why can projecting away gpa prevent a later grade selection?
options: Projection automatically remembers every hidden role
WHERE creates missing columns
All operations commute unconditionally
The later condition no longer has its required attribute
questions.explanation: A rewrite must retain inputs needed by later predicates.

questions.question_text: Does projection delete source columns?
options: No; it derives an output with selected roles
Yes; it runs ALTER TABLE
Only if DISTINCT appears
Only if the output is empty
questions.explanation: Query result structure and persistent schema differ.

questions.question_text: What does a distinct student department projection omit?
options: Every active department always
Catalogue departments unrepresented in its student input
All duplicate-free values
Every selected attribute name
questions.explanation: The source population is not automatically a complete catalogue.

questions.question_text: Can projection reduce cardinality without a row predicate?
options: No; only selection can change counts
Only if source data is deleted
Yes; equal selected tuples collapse under set semantics
Only if names are missing
questions.explanation: Duplicate elimination differs from predicate filtering.

questions.question_text: What makes a fixed explicit SELECT list useful to callers?
options: It enforces every foreign key
It grants access automatically
It sorts rows automatically
Its output roles and order remain stated despite unrelated source additions
questions.explanation: Output shape is a contract distinct from source width.

questions.question_text: Does SQL DISTINCT have defined NULL behaviour?
options: Yes; it is not governed solely by ordinary NULL equality predicates
No; duplicate elimination is undefined
Only for keys
Only if all values are numeric
questions.explanation: Different operations have specified absence semantics.

questions.question_text: How can a report exclude absent departments before distinct projection?
options: Use department = NULL
Use WHERE department IS NOT NULL
Assume DISTINCT removes every NULL automatically
Rename NULL as zero universally
questions.explanation: The population predicate states the absence policy.

questions.question_text: What is the degree of an empty result selecting two attributes?
options: Zero
The original row count
Two
Undefined because no rows exist
questions.explanation: The result still has its selected structure.

questions.question_text: Does a client projection establish protected-column authorization?
options: Yes; selecting one label secures every other endpoint
Only with DISTINCT
Only if sorted
No; trusted access rules need separate enforcement
questions.explanation: Data minimization and authorization are different guarantees.

coding_problems.title: Return the represented department set
coding_problems.task: Return each distinct department value present among students exactly once. Do not include student_id or campus in the output.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, department VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, campus VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, active INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.ordering: Department ascending, then campus ascending when selected.
constraints: Department and campus values are nonmissing canonical labels; active is 0 or 1.
edge_cases: Several identities can share the selected values.
Different campuses can preserve distinct department-campus pairs.
hints: Use DISTINCT when the requested grain is a set of combinations.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT DISTINCT department FROM students ORDER BY department;
coding_problems.explanation: The selected tuple and explicit duplicate policy determine the result grain independently of source student identity.

coding_problems.title: Project the active department-campus combinations
coding_problems.task: Return distinct department and campus pairs represented by active students only. A department in two campuses produces two pairs; several active students in the same pair produce one.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, department VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, campus VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, active INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.expected:
department	campus
Computing	North
Computing	South
History	South
coding_problems.ordering: Department ascending, then campus ascending when selected.
constraints: Department and campus values are nonmissing canonical labels; active is 0 or 1.
edge_cases: Several identities can share the selected values.
Different campuses can preserve distinct department-campus pairs.
hints: Use DISTINCT when the requested grain is a set of combinations.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT DISTINCT department, campus FROM students WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY department, campus;
coding_problems.explanation: The selected tuple and explicit duplicate policy determine the result grain independently of source student identity.
